title: Fasting is prescribed
hookLine: the fast of Ramadan is ordained in the second year (2:183)

lines: A DATE AND WATER AT SUNSET.
cards: Before dawn, a quick meal in a quiet kitchen. Then nothing to eat or drink until sunset. Office workers in London.
Farmers in Indonesia. Students in Chicago, slipping out of a lecture to break the fast with a date and a bottle of water. Grandmothers cooking all afternoon for food they can't taste yet.
Every Ramadan, a month of days like that. But it had a first year. In Medina, after the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ arrived, a verse came down that started all of it.

teach.b: In Pickthall's translation: "O ye who believe! Fasting is prescribed for you, even as it was prescribed for those before you, that ye may ward off (evil)." Three things in one line.
Prescribed: kutiba, written, the way a rule is written down. Before you: this isn't new.
Before Ramadan, the Prophet had fasted on the day of 'Ashura, and Sahih al-Bukhari says the Jews of Medina fasted that day too, remembering Moses being saved.
After Ramadan was prescribed, 'Ashura stayed as a fast people could choose.

teach.h: THAT YOU MAY WARD OFF EVIL.
teach.b: And the reason: that you may ward off evil, or as it's often explained, that you may gain taqwa, the careful awareness of God we've met before. Teachers often explain that the fast isn't about hunger for its own sake.
It's practice in saying no to what you want, so you can say no to worse things. The next verses fill in the kindness. A fixed number of days.
If you're sick or traveling, make the days up later. They speak of feeding a poor person as a ransom, which scholars apply to those who can't fast at all.
Then the line: God wants ease for you, not hardship.
The month is Ramadan, the verses say, the month in which the Qur'an was sent down. Tradition dates this command to the second year after the migration.
So the very first Ramadan fast happened in that plain little city, in a mosque of palm trunks.

how: Muslims fast every day of Ramadan from dawn to sunset, with a pre-dawn meal (suhur) and a meal at sunset (iftar); the sick, travelers, and others excused make up the days later or feed the poor, and some also fast voluntarily on Mondays and Thursdays.

o: it is a burden: heavy and hard to carry
it is optional: left for you to choose
it is written: set down like a rule

games.q: what's inside the verse — tap the pairs.

s: the verse says fasting is new, only for Muslims
prescribed for you, even as it was prescribed for those before you.
the sick are excused and make up the days later
the verses say so, and add: God wants ease for you, not hardship.
tradition dates it to the second year after the migration, in Medina.

games.q: the fast of Ramadan has just been prescribed. you're traveling a long way. what do the verses say?
o: you may break it, and make the days up later.
games.why: travelers and the sick make up the days later. God wants ease for you, the verses say, not hardship.

practice: Only if fasting is safe for your body, since the verses themselves excuse the sick, choose a day for one voluntary fast; at-Tirmidhi records that the Prophet made a habit of fasting on Mondays and Thursdays, and some Muslims keep it.
Picture the pre-dawn meal, the long afternoon, the first sip of water at sunset. If a food fast isn't right for you, choose one thing to go without from dawn to sunset instead.

wordCard.voice: Kutiba, it is written: the word in 2:183 that wrote the fast of Ramadan for Muslims, as it was written for those before them.

orig.note: Arabic: fasting is prescribed for you (2:183). kutiba: it is written.

carryVoice: Your line: prescribed for you. Written for them, as for those before. Day two hundred sixty-three, done.

sources.q: O ye who believe! Fasting is prescribed for you, even as it was prescribed for those before you, that ye may ward off (evil).

sources.ref: Qur'an 2:184–185 (a fixed number of days; the sick and travelers; feeding the poor; ease, not hardship; the month the Qur'an was sent down)
Sahih al-Bukhari 2002, 2004 ('Ashura before Ramadan; the Jews of Medina fasting it for Moses)
